screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Dovecot is the standard Mail Delivery Agent for Linux systems and how it enables IMAP and POP3 client access. We’ll clarify the distinct roles of the MTA and the MDA so you understand when Postfix hands off mail and when Dovecot presents mail to a user. You will see how Maildir differs from mbox, why Maildir is the recommended choice for robustness and concurrency, and how Dovecot’s modular configuration files control mail location and authentication. Throughout, I’ll highlight common mistakes — like incorrect mail_location or forgetting to reload Dovecot — and a quick security reminder about plaintext authentication in lab versus production. By the end, you’ll know how to perform an initial Dovecot deployment that’s ready for further hardening.

screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on verification, safety, and common mistakes you should watch for. You will practice opening IMAP and POP3 ports in your firewall so clients can reach Dovecot, and you will run practical connectivity tests using telnet for plain IMAP or openssl s_client for TLS-protected IMAPS. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Testing & Safety
Safety and Verification Checklist
A compact checklist to validate connectivity, configuration, and authentication choices before you move to production.
Quick Tests
Start and enable Dovecot
sudo systemctl enable --now dovecot
sudo systemctl status dovecot
Firewall ports
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=imap --add-service=imaps
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=pop3 --add-service=pop3s
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Connectivity checks
telnet your_mail_server_ip 143
# or
openssl s_client -connect your_mail_server_ip:993
Common Pitfalls
  • Wrong mail_location path prevents Dovecot from finding mail.
  • Not reloading Dovecot after edits means changes won't apply.
  • Firewall blocking IMAP/POP3 ports prevents client connections.
  • User accounts missing or passwords are incorrect for PAM auth.

screens.title: What is Dovecot and the MDA role?
screens.narratorSegment: Dovecot is a Mail Delivery Agent and IMAP/POP3 server used on Linux to present user mailboxes to clients like Thunderbird or Outlook. The MDA is responsible for local delivery and mailbox management while the MTA — typically Postfix — moves mail between servers. This separation is important: the MTA focuses on transport and routing, and the MDA focuses on storage, indexing, and secure client access. Dovecot provides both IMAP, for server-side message management and synchronization, and POP3, for downloading messages to clients. The practical distinction matters when designing mail systems: if users access mail from multiple devices you should prefer IMAP so state and folders remain consistent across clients. As an administrator, knowing the MDA role helps you decide where to apply policies, storage choices, and authentication methods. For example, Postfix hands off an incoming message to the local delivery agent; Dovecot then places that message into the user’s mailbox and serves it to authenticated clients. A common misconception is thinking the MTA alone stores and serves mail to clients — in reality the MDA is the mailbox authority. Remember: Dovecot manages mailbox format, access protocols, and authentication, making it the core piece that clients interact with.

keyIdea.text: Dovecot is the MDA and IMAP/POP3 server that manages user mailboxes and presents mail to clients; MTAs handle transport between servers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Core Concept
What is Dovecot and the MDA role?
Understand why Dovecot, not the MTA, manages user mailboxes and client access.
Definition and responsibilities
  • Accept local delivery from the MTA and place messages into mailboxes.
  • Serve mail to clients via IMAP and POP3 protocols.
  • Manage indexing, mailbox format, and access permissions.
Analogy
Think of Postfix as the postal service moving letters between offices; Dovecot is the local post office that stores mail for recipients and lets them retrieve it securely.
Example scenario
An incoming email is routed by Postfix to the local delivery agent. Dovecot stores it in the user's Maildir and allows the user's IMAP client to mark it read and move it to a folder. Those changes are visible from other clients because Dovecot manages server-side state.
Common misconception
Do not assume the MTA provides mailbox browsing. The MTA delivers; the MDA stores and serves mail to MUAs. Confusing these leads to configuration errors and broken client access.
Key Takeaway

Dovecot is the mailbox authority; configure it for storage format, access protocols, and authentication to ensure reliable client access.

screens.title: IMAP versus POP3
screens.narratorSegment: IMAP and POP3 are two older but still important mail retrieval protocols. IMAP is designed for server-side management: messages remain on the server and clients synchronize state such as read flags and folder structure. This makes IMAP the preferred modern protocol because it supports multiple clients accessing the same mailbox with a consistent view. POP3, by contrast, is a simpler download protocol: it retrieves messages from the server to the client and often deletes them from the server afterwards. POP3 can be useful for single-device setups or constrained environments, but it does not provide synchronized state across devices. A useful mental model is IMAP as remote mail management and POP3 as a one-time download. When deploying Dovecot for modern users, configure IMAP as the primary service. In practice, this means ensuring Dovecot listens on port 143 for IMAP and 993 for IMAPS while making POP3 optional on ports 110 and 995. A common mistake is enabling plaintext authentication over POP3 without TLS; for production, require TLS and set disable_plaintext_auth to yes so credentials are never sent unencrypted. Which protocol you choose directly affects folder behavior, user expectations, and how you plan backups and storage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Comparison
IMAP versus POP3
Decide which protocol matches your user needs and client expectations.
IMAP (Server-side)
  • Messages remain on the server and clients sync state.
  • Supports multiple clients and shared folder state.
  • Ports: 143 (IMAP), 993 (IMAPS).
Use IMAP for modern deployments where users access mail from many devices and expect synchronized folders and read states.
POP3 (Download)
  • Designed to download messages to a client and often remove them from the server.
  • Less suitable for multi-device access and shared state.
  • Ports: 110 (POP3), 995 (POP3S).
Use POP3 only for single-device or legacy scenarios where server-side state is not required.
Example

If a user reads mail on a phone and a laptop and expects folders to match, configure IMAP so both clients see the same state.

Misconception

Don’t assume POP3 provides the same synchronized folder behavior as IMAP; it generally does not.

screens.title: Install and start Dovecot
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Dovecot is a straightforward first step in the lab. On Red Hat-based distributions use the package manager to install dovecot and then enable and start the service so it accepts client connections. Verifying the service status confirms the daemon is running and listening. These steps are essential because installation alone does not guarantee the service is enabled to start automatically after reboot. In a lab you should run the package install command, then enable and start Dovecot with systemctl, and finally check the unit’s status for active (running). If there are dependency errors or SELinux denials they will usually appear in the status output, giving a clear troubleshooting path. Remember to reload or restart Dovecot after you edit configuration files so your changes take effect. A common error is editing files but never reloading the daemon, which leaves the previous configuration active. Performing the install, enable, and status sequence gives you a known good baseline before changing mail_location or authentication settings. Install and start Dovecot means install the dovecot package, enable and start the service, and check systemctl status to confirm it is active before making configuration changes.. In practical terms, package install, enable service, and verify health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Process Flow
Install and start Dovecot
Follow this minimal install sequence to get Dovecot up and running for testing.
Commands (RHEL example)
sudo dnf install dovecot -y
sudo systemctl enable --now dovecot
sudo systemctl status dovecot
Run these commands as root or with sudo. The status output helps you detect common startup issues before proceeding to configuration edits.
Checklist
  • Package installed successfully.
  • Service enabled and running.
  • No SELinux or permission errors in status output.
Tip
If you see errors, check journalctl for dovecot logs and verify file permissions on configuration files.

screens.title: Dovecot configuration files
screens.narratorSegment: Dovecot uses a modular configuration model with a main file and multiple smaller includes under /etc/dovecot/conf. d/. The primary central file often seen is /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf, but most settings live in numbered files such as 10-mail. conf, 10-auth. conf, and 10-master. conf. This modular approach makes targeted edits safer and easier to manage because each file holds related settings: 10-mail. conf controls mail_location and storage format, 10-auth. conf defines authentication options and which mechanisms to enable, and 10-master. conf controls service listeners and master process behavior. Knowing the file responsible for a setting prevents the common mistake of editing the wrong file and wondering why changes do not take effect. After changing a file, reload or restart Dovecot so the daemon reads the updated configuration. In production you should keep backups of original files and use configuration management to apply consistent settings. For a lab, focus your edits in the specific conf. d files mentioned by name so you can quickly revert or verify a single change if troubleshooting becomes necessary. Dovecot configuration files means dovecot configuration is modular; edit the specific 10-*.conf file for mail and auth to make focused, reversible changes.. In practical terms, understanding the modular layout: dovecot.conf and conf.d/*. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Configuration
Dovecot configuration files
Locate settings quickly by editing the appropriate 10-*.conf file.
Key files
  • /etc/dovecot/dovecot.conf (main include)
  • /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-mail.conf (mail_location)
  • /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-auth.conf (authentication)
  • /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-master.conf (listeners/processes)
Why modularity helps
Modular files let you change a single responsibility without touching unrelated settings. For example, set mail_location in 10-mail.conf and authentication methods in 10-auth.conf. This reduces the blast radius of edits and simplifies audits and rollbacks.
Practical tip
Use grep to confirm your change: grep -E "mail_location|disable_plaintext_auth|auth_mechanisms" /etc/dovecot/conf.d/*

screens.title: Mail storage: mbox versus Maildir
screens.narratorSegment: A critical decision for mailbox storage is choosing between mbox and Maildir. mbox stores all messages for a user in a single file, often located under /var/spool/mail/username. This single-file approach can be simple, but it becomes fragile with large mailboxes or concurrent access because multiple processes touching the same file raise corruption risk. Maildir uses a directory structure where each message is a separate file typically stored in ~/Maildir with subdirectories new, cur, and tmp. This layout avoids shared-file contention, improves performance for concurrent access, and makes recovery of individual messages simpler. For these reasons Maildir is recommended for modern mail servers and is the configuration we will use in the lab. If the Maildir does not exist, Dovecot can create it on first delivery or when a client connects. A common misstep is pointing mail_location to an incorrect path or format; ensure the syntax maildir:~/Maildir is used when you want per-user Maildir storage. Choosing Maildir reduces corruption risk and simplifies scaling for multiple simultaneous client connections. In practical terms, why maildir is preferred for modern deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Definition
Mail storage: mbox versus Maildir
Understand the storage formats and why Maildir is usually better for servers handling multiple clients.
mbox
Stores all messages in a single file. Simpler but prone to corruption and poor concurrent performance for large mailboxes.
Maildir
Stores each message as a file in ~/Maildir/new, ~/Maildir/cur, and ~/Maildir/tmp. More robust and recommended for modern servers.
Example

Set mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir so Dovecot creates and uses per-user Maildir directories under their home folders.

Pitfall

Pointing mail_location to the wrong format or path prevents Dovecot from finding mail and causes client failures.

screens.title: Configure Maildir in 10-mail.conf
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Dovecot to use Maildir is a single-line change but it has important effects on where mail is stored and how clients interact with it. Edit /etc/dovecot/conf. d/10-mail. conf and set mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir. This instructs Dovecot to look for a Maildir directory inside each user’s home directory. If a Maildir does not exist, Dovecot will normally create it upon the first delivery or when a client connects and requests folder listing. After making the change, reload Dovecot so it reads the updated setting. Verify the configuration with a grep of the conf. d files to confirm the mail_location line is present. A typical mistake is using an incorrect prefix or path, for example mixing mbox syntax with Maildir or pointing to a system spool directory when user home paths are intended. Also confirm filesystem permissions allow Dovecot to access and create Maildir directories in user homes. This one configuration step improves mailbox reliability by storing each message separately and reduces the risk of corruption from concurrent access. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Configuration
Configure Maildir in 10-mail.conf
A single setting that ensures Dovecot uses Maildir storage under each user's home.
Edit file
# /etc/dovecot/conf.d/10-mail.conf
mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir
Save the file and then reload Dovecot so the change takes effect: sudo systemctl reload dovecot
Checks
  • grep -E "mail_location" /etc/dovecot/conf.d/*

screens.title: Open IMAP/POP3 ports in the firewall
screens.narratorSegment: Network access is a simple but common stumbling block: Dovecot must be reachable on the standard IMAP and POP3 ports. For Red Hat-based systems using firewalld, add the imap and imaps services plus pop3 and pop3s as permanent services and reload the firewall so the rules persist. For Debian/Ubuntu systems using ufw, allow the IMAP, IMAPS, POP3, and POP3S profiles and reload. A common error is opening ports only temporarily or forgetting to reload the firewall, which leads to intermittent connectivity during testing. screens.title: Create a test user and verify IMAP connectivity

screens.title: Common mistakes and production notes
screens.narratorSegment: When deploying Dovecot, several recurring mistakes can prevent client access or cause mailbox corruption. The most frequent issues are incorrect mail_location settings, not reloading Dovecot after edits, firewall rules blocking ports, and missing or misconfigured user accounts for authentication. Maildir versus mbox mistakes often appear when administrators mix format syntax or point to a spool path that Dovecot cannot write to. Another important production note is authentication scaling: while PAM and system users are convenient for labs, production deployments tend to use virtual users or LDAP for manageability and isolation. Security is also critical: never leave plaintext authentication enabled without TLS in production. Instead, set disable_plaintext_auth = yes and enable IMAPS/POP3S so credentials travel encrypted. Finally, automated configuration management and backups of the conf. d directory make rollbacks simpler and reduce human error. These practical checks and choices help you move from a working lab configuration into a supportable and secure production posture. screens.title: What to Remember

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Dovecot is the standard Mail Delivery Agent for Linux systems and how it enables IMAP and POP3 client access. We’ll clarify the distinct roles of the MTA and the MDA so you understand when Postfix hands off mail and when Dovecot presents mail to a user. You will see how Maildir differs from mbox, why Maildir is the recommended choice for robustness and concurrency, and how Dovecot’s modular configuration files control mail location and authentication. You will also follow a safe lab sequence: install Dovecot, enable the service, set mail_location to Maildir, allow basic PAM authentication for testing, open IMAP and POP3 ports in the firewall, and verify access using a test system user and simple connectivity checks. Throughout, I’ll highlight common mistakes — like incorrect mail_location or forgetting to reload Dovecot — and a quick security reminder about plaintext authentication in lab versus production. By the end, you’ll know how to perform an initial Dovecot deployment that’s ready for further hardening.

By the end of this chapter you will understand the MDA’s role and be able to install and perform an initial configuration of Dovecot for IMAP and POP3 access. You will configure Dovecot to use Maildir storage so mail is stored as one file per message, which reduces corruption and improves concurrency compared with mbox. You will enable basic authentication using system accounts via PAM for quick lab testing and learn why plaintext authentication must be disabled in production. You will also open the necessary firewall ports to permit IMAP and POP3 traffic and verify service operation with simple client checks such as telnet or openssl s_client. Each objective links a configuration task to a practical reason: robust mailbox storage, reliable user authentication, and verifiable network access. These skills matter because they form the baseline for a usable mail service and allow you to later harden authentication or move to virtual users without breaking client access during migration.

This second objectives slide focuses on verification, safety, and common mistakes you should watch for. You will practice opening IMAP and POP3 ports in your firewall so clients can reach Dovecot, and you will run practical connectivity tests using telnet for plain IMAP or openssl s_client for TLS-protected IMAPS. You will also learn to reload Dovecot after configuration changes and verify the service with systemctl status. Importantly, you will recognize common configuration errors such as incorrect mail_location values, missing user accounts, or forgetting to reload the service after edits. Finally, you will contrast lab-safe configurations — like allowing plaintext authentication temporarily — with production requirements, where disable_plaintext_auth must be yes and TLS should be enforced. These checks help you build a repeatable lab procedure and avoid the small mistakes that often block client logins during a deployment.

Dovecot is a Mail Delivery Agent and IMAP/POP3 server used on Linux to present user mailboxes to clients like Thunderbird or Outlook. The MDA is responsible for local delivery and mailbox management while the MTA — typically Postfix — moves mail between servers. This separation is important: the MTA focuses on transport and routing, and the MDA focuses on storage, indexing, and secure client access. Dovecot provides both IMAP, for server-side message management and synchronization, and POP3, for downloading messages to clients. The practical distinction matters when designing mail systems: if users access mail from multiple devices you should prefer IMAP so state and folders remain consistent across clients. As an administrator, knowing the MDA role helps you decide where to apply policies, storage choices, and authentication methods. For example, Postfix hands off an incoming message to the local delivery agent; Dovecot then places that message into the user’s mailbox and serves it to authenticated clients. A common misconception is thinking the MTA alone stores and serves mail to clients — in reality the MDA is the mailbox authority. Remember: Dovecot manages mailbox format, access protocols, and authentication, making it the core piece that clients interact with.

IMAP and POP3 are two older but still important mail retrieval protocols. IMAP is designed for server-side management: messages remain on the server and clients synchronize state such as read flags and folder structure. This makes IMAP the preferred modern protocol because it supports multiple clients accessing the same mailbox with a consistent view. POP3, by contrast, is a simpler download protocol: it retrieves messages from the server to the client and often deletes them from the server afterwards. POP3 can be useful for single-device setups or constrained environments, but it does not provide synchronized state across devices. A useful mental model is IMAP as remote mail management and POP3 as a one-time download. When deploying Dovecot for modern users, configure IMAP as the primary service. In practice, this means ensuring Dovecot listens on port 143 for IMAP and 993 for IMAPS while making POP3 optional on ports 110 and 995. A common mistake is enabling plaintext authentication over POP3 without TLS; for production, require TLS and set disable_plaintext_auth to yes so credentials are never sent unencrypted. Which protocol you choose directly affects folder behavior, user expectations, and how you plan backups and storage.

Installing Dovecot is a straightforward first step in the lab. On Red Hat-based distributions use the package manager to install dovecot and then enable and start the service so it accepts client connections. Verifying the service status confirms the daemon is running and listening. These steps are essential because installation alone does not guarantee the service is enabled to start automatically after reboot. In a lab you should run the package install command, then enable and start Dovecot with systemctl, and finally check the unit’s status for active (running). If there are dependency errors or SELinux denials they will usually appear in the status output, giving a clear troubleshooting path. Remember to reload or restart Dovecot after you edit configuration files so your changes take effect. A common error is editing files but never reloading the daemon, which leaves the previous configuration active. Performing the install, enable, and status sequence gives you a known good baseline before changing mail_location or authentication settings. Install and start Dovecot means install the dovecot package, enable and start the service, and check systemctl status to confirm it is active before making configuration changes.. In practical terms, package install, enable service, and verify health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dovecot uses a modular configuration model with a main file and multiple smaller includes under /etc/dovecot/conf. d/. The primary central file often seen is /etc/dovecot/dovecot. conf, but most settings live in numbered files such as 10-mail. conf, 10-auth. conf, and 10-master. conf. This modular approach makes targeted edits safer and easier to manage because each file holds related settings: 10-mail. conf controls mail_location and storage format, 10-auth. conf defines authentication options and which mechanisms to enable, and 10-master. conf controls service listeners and master process behavior. Knowing the file responsible for a setting prevents the common mistake of editing the wrong file and wondering why changes do not take effect. After changing a file, reload or restart Dovecot so the daemon reads the updated configuration. In production you should keep backups of original files and use configuration management to apply consistent settings. For a lab, focus your edits in the specific conf. d files mentioned by name so you can quickly revert or verify a single change if troubleshooting becomes necessary. Dovecot configuration files means dovecot configuration is modular; edit the specific 10-*.conf file for mail and auth to make focused, reversible changes.. In practical terms, understanding the modular layout: dovecot.conf and conf.d/*. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A critical decision for mailbox storage is choosing between mbox and Maildir. mbox stores all messages for a user in a single file, often located under /var/spool/mail/username. This single-file approach can be simple, but it becomes fragile with large mailboxes or concurrent access because multiple processes touching the same file raise corruption risk. Maildir uses a directory structure where each message is a separate file typically stored in ~/Maildir with subdirectories new, cur, and tmp. This layout avoids shared-file contention, improves performance for concurrent access, and makes recovery of individual messages simpler. For these reasons Maildir is recommended for modern mail servers and is the configuration we will use in the lab. If the Maildir does not exist, Dovecot can create it on first delivery or when a client connects. A common misstep is pointing mail_location to an incorrect path or format; ensure the syntax maildir:~/Maildir is used when you want per-user Maildir storage. Choosing Maildir reduces corruption risk and simplifies scaling for multiple simultaneous client connections. Mail storage: mbox versus Maildir means maildir stores each message as an individual file, providing better concurrency and robustness than single-file mbox storage.. In practical terms, why maildir is preferred for modern deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuring Dovecot to use Maildir is a single-line change but it has important effects on where mail is stored and how clients interact with it. Edit /etc/dovecot/conf. d/10-mail. conf and set mail_location = maildir:~/Maildir. This instructs Dovecot to look for a Maildir directory inside each user’s home directory. If a Maildir does not exist, Dovecot will normally create it upon the first delivery or when a client connects and requests folder listing. After making the change, reload Dovecot so it reads the updated setting. Verify the configuration with a grep of the conf. d files to confirm the mail_location line is present. A typical mistake is using an incorrect prefix or path, for example mixing mbox syntax with Maildir or pointing to a system spool directory when user home paths are intended. Also confirm filesystem permissions allow Dovecot to access and create Maildir directories in user homes. This one configuration step improves mailbox reliability by storing each message separately and reduces the risk of corruption from concurrent access. Configure Maildir in 10-mail.conf means add mail_location = maildir:~/maildir to 10-mail.conf and reload dovecot; ensure permissions and path correctness.. In practical terms, set mail_location and ensure maildir creation and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Here are the three essential concepts to carry forward. First, Dovecot is the Mail Delivery Agent and IMAP/POP3 server that stores mail and serves it to clients; the MTA moves mail between servers while the MDA manages mailbox format and client access. Third, authentication and security matter: PAM-based system-user authentication is convenient in labs, but do not leave plaintext authentication enabled in production; instead require TLS and consider virtual users or LDAP for scalable, secure deployments.
